title: UFO Investigator Claims 700 Alien Abductions Stopped Dead in Their Tracks by Calling on Jesus' Name
excerpt: Florida UFO investigator Joe Jordan says more than 700 people reported that alleged alien-abduction experiences ended after they invoked Jesus, but scientists cite alternative explanations including sleep paralysis and false memories.
content:
A UFO investigator claims he has worked with more than 700 people who say their alleged alien-abduction experiences stopped after they called on the name of Jesus Christ.

Joe Jordan, a Florida-based UFO investigator and founder of the CE4 Research Group, says he began documenting these accounts after encountering people who reported that an apparent abduction ended suddenly when they invoked Jesus. In a July 2026 interview, Jordan said he had dealt with 'well over 700' case histories since 1997.

The claim does not establish that extraterrestrial beings exist or that the reported experiences were genuine physical abductions.

Jordan's accounts are based on testimony from people who interpret their experiences that way, while researchers have proposed explanations ranging from sleep paralysis and hallucinations to memory and cultural influences.

Jordan Says Invoking Jesus Ended the Experiences

Jordan's interest in the phenomenon dates back to his work investigating UFO reports. According to material from his CE4 Research Group, he began receiving accounts in the 1990s from people who said they had experienced what they understood to be alien encounters and that the events stopped after they called upon Jesus Christ.

The organisation says it has worked with more than 400 so-called alien-abduction cases in which people reported that invoking Jesus ended the experience. Jordan has separately said the number of case histories he has personally dealt with has since risen to more than 700.

The accounts reportedly involve experiences commonly associated with alleged abductions, including paralysis, frightening figures, a perceived loss of control and the sensation of being taken or examined.

Jordan interprets the pattern through a Christian framework and has argued that the phenomenon may have a spiritual rather than extraterrestrial explanation.

That interpretation remains disputed, and the available accounts are based on testimony rather than independently verified evidence of extraterrestrial activity.

Researchers Have Proposed Alternative Explanations

Research into alleged alien-abduction experiences has identified sleep paralysis as one possible explanation for at least some reports. During sleep paralysis, a person can become conscious while temporarily unable to move, and the experience can include vivid hallucinations, including the sensation that another presence is nearby.

A 2005 study by researchers Richard McNally and Susan Clancy examined 10 people who reported alien-abduction experiences and found that their accounts were linked to apparent episodes of sleep paralysis in which hypnopompic hallucinations were interpreted as alien beings.

A review published in Cognitive Neuropsychiatry also examined sleep paralysis and false-memory research as possible clues to alien-abduction experiences, while concluding that further research was needed.

Those explanations do not directly test Jordan's claim that some people report their experiences ending specifically after invoking Jesus.

Instead, they offer possible explanations for some of the underlying experiences and raise a separate question about whether invoking Jesus caused the reported experience to stop, or whether changes in expectation, fear and consciousness influenced how the experience was perceived.

Why the 700 Cases Remain Controversial

The sheer number of testimonies is what gives Jordan's claim its continuing appeal, but testimony alone cannot establish what physically happened during the reported encounters. Jordan says he has spent decades collecting these accounts and making them available through his research.

His CE4 material describes the cases as part of an effort to investigate what he regards as an overlooked aspect of the UFO phenomenon. The distinction matters because there is currently no established scientific evidence demonstrating that extraterrestrial beings abduct humans or that saying Jesus' name physically prevents such encounters.

For people who accept the experiences as spiritual events, however, the testimonies have a different significance. Jordan continues to present them as evidence that the phenomenon may not fit neatly into an extraterrestrial explanation.

For now, the 700-plus figure is best understood as Jordan's reported case-history total, rather than a verified count of alien abductions. The accounts remain part of the wider debate over whether alleged abduction experiences are paranormal events, psychological phenomena, sleep-related experiences or something science has yet to explain.
